content.title: About
content.content: Tomatoes, canned, cooked are whole or diced tomatoes that have been heat‑treated and sealed in glass or metal jars with added salt, tomato paste, spices and sometimes sugar. The product is ready to eat and is commonly used in sauces, soups, stews and many other dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Canning preserves the flavor and most nutrients of tomatoes for months or years.
Canned tomatoes are usually blanched first, which makes skin removal easy.
In the United States, canned tomatoes are one of the “five basic vegetables” frequently served in school meals.
Tomatoes can be “pelleted” – ground into a puree that simplifies later cooking.
Thermal processing increases the bioavailability of lycopene compared with fresh tomatoes.

items.title: Rich in lycopene
items.content: Lycopene is a powerful antioxidant that supports heart health and may lower the risk of certain cancers.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Dietary fiber in tomatoes promotes healthy bowel function and satiety.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Canned tomatoes are a low‑calorie food, suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and supports muscle function.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some canned tomato varieties contain added salt, which may be a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Bisphenol A (BPA)
items.content: Cans lined with BPA can leach chemicals; choose BPA‑free or glass containers when possible.

items.title: Tomato allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to tomatoes.

items.title: Added sugar
items.content: Certain recipes add sugar to balance acidity; this should be considered for sugar‑controlled diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned tomatoes can be added to pasta sauces, soups, chili, stews, pizza, and salads. They also serve as a base for tomato juice or paste. The product is ready to eat, but you may heat it if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened jars in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the contents in a sealed container in the refrigerator and use within 5‑7 days. Discard if the jar is bulging, leaking, or the tomatoes develop an off‑odor.
